title: Matthew 13:44–46
context: Jesus pairs two brief kingdom images: treasure hidden in the field and a merchant found one pearl of great value—both ending in joyful, total exchange for what is found.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Classic Arminian and Reformed comment on Matthew 13:44–46, in the writers’ own words.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: The three following parables are proposed, not to the multitude, but peculiarly to the apostles: the two former of them relate to those who receive the Gospel; the third, both to those who receive, and those who preach it. The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hid in a field - The kingdom of God within us is a treasure indeed, but a treasure hid from the world, and from the most wise and prudent in it.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on Matt 13:44–46)

reformed.quote: The first two of these parables are intended to instruct believers to prefer the Kingdom of heaven to the whole world, and therefore to deny themselves and all the desires of the flesh, that nothing may prevent them from obtaining so valuable a possession. We are greatly in need of such a warning; for we are so captivated by the allurements of the world, that eternal life fades from our view; and in consequence of our carnality, the spiritual graces of God are far from being held by us in the estimation which they deserve.
reformed.source: Commentary on a Harmony of the Evangelists (on Matt 13:44–46)

verses.text: “Again, the Kingdom of Heaven is like treasure hidden in the field, which a man found and hid. In his joy, he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field.
verses.arminianNotes:
Hidden treasure, found and covered, then sold-all purchase in joy. The kingdom’s worth reorders every lesser claim.

Arminian readers hear a sincere summons to count the cost and still choose Christ. Grace enables the joyful exchange; the response of selling all remains a glad act of trust.
verses.reformedNotes:
The kingdom is treasure worth everything. Joy fuels the sale of all lesser goods for the field that holds it.

God awakens desire for the surpassing worth of His kingdom. The man’s joy and total exchange display a heart God has claimed.
verses.keyContrast: Both treat the kingdom as worth total surrender. Arminians emphasize grace-enabled, responsible joyful exchange; Reformed readers emphasize God’s effectual awakening of delight that makes selling all inevitable for those He draws.

verses.text: “Again, the Kingdom of Heaven is like a man who is a merchant seeking fine pearls,
verses.arminianNotes:
A merchant searching for fine pearls pictures earnest seeking. The kingdom meets those who look for excellence and find more than they expected.

Seeking is not unbelief; grace often works through honest search until the true pearl appears.
verses.reformedNotes:
Search precedes finding. The merchant’s vocation becomes a kingdom parable under Christ’s word.

God may use human seeking as the path along which He discloses the one pearl that ends the hunt.

verses.text: who having found one pearl of great price, he went and sold all that he had and bought it.
verses.arminianNotes:
One pearl of great value ends the search: sell all, buy it. Singularity matters—many fine pearls, one supreme.

Do not settle for lesser pearls. Assisting grace enables the decisive purchase of Christ and His kingdom above every rival.
verses.reformedNotes:
Finding leads to total divestment and purchase. The pearl’s value creates the economy of the exchange.

When God shows the pearl, lesser treasures lose their hold. Saving discovery is His gift that reorders the whole life.
verses.keyContrast: Both see exclusive worth in the one pearl. Arminians typically underline a grace-enabled decisive choice; Reformed readers stress God’s revelatory gift that effectually reorders what the heart will sell.
